core: What counts as a community: geographic, identity-based, and functional definitions, and why the boundary decision is consequential
Who is authorised to speak for a community, and the failure mode of consulting only the already-organised
Rothman's threefold typology of community intervention (locality development, social planning, social action) with correct attribution
Rothman's own 2007 revision of the typology into multiple overlapping modes (capacity development, social planning/policy, advocacy)
Community organising traditions, including Alinsky's model and later critiques of professionalised, grant-dependent organising
Asset-based community development (Kretzmann and McKnight) and asset mapping as the community-scale analogue of a strengths perspective, plus its structural critique
The community needs assessment as a formal method, including the community health needs assessment required of tax-exempt hospital facilities
Community-based participatory research: the community as partner rather than study site, and the observed gap between that ideal and practice
Coalition building, the factors associated with coalition effectiveness, and predictable failure modes
Power analysis and stakeholder mapping as planning tools
Evaluation of community practice: what the evidence supports, what it does not, and why causal attribution at community scale is hard
supporting: Top-down and bottom-up approaches to community change and the trade-off between resources and legitimacy
Iatrogenic effects and unintended consequences of outside partnership
Sustainability: grant-funded projects and services that end when funding ends
The Accountable Health Communities Model as a large, evaluated test of connecting people to community resources
outOfScope: Case-versus-cause advocacy and lobbying rules for tax-exempt organisations (owned by the advocacy topic)
The policy process, policy analysis, and how bills become programmes (owned by social-policy-and-human-services)
Poverty measurement, the Official Poverty Measure and SPM, and concentrated poverty as a measured phenomenon (owned by poverty-and-social-inequality)
Individual assessment method, screening instruments, and service planning (owned by needs-assessment)
Individualised legal, political, organisational, or clinical advice
Any evaluation of, or position on, a political party, movement, or ideology

claims.claim: Community can be defined by geography, by shared identity or perspective, or by joint action, and an interview study across four very different populations found five recurring elements: locus, sharing, joint action, social ties, and diversity, weighted differently by different groups.

MacQueen and colleagues derived a common definition of community as a group of people with diverse characteristics linked by social ties, sharing common perspectives, and engaging in joint action in geographical locations or settings, drawn from 118 interviews conducted 1995-1998 with African Americans in Durham, gay men in San Francisco, injection drug users in Philadelphia, and HIV vaccine researchers.

Where a community boundary is drawn has legal consequences: U.S. Treasury regulations let a tax-exempt hospital facility define the community it serves by geography, target population, or principal function, but forbid it from defining that community so as to exclude medically underserved, low-income, or minority populations living in the areas from which it draws patients.

A tax-exempt hospital facility must conduct a community health needs assessment in the taxable year or either of the two preceding years, and an authorised body must adopt an implementation strategy; the required steps are defining the community served, assessing its health needs, soliciting and taking into account input from persons representing the broad interests of the community, documenting the assessment in a written report adopted by an authorised body, and making that report widely available to the public.

Assessing community health needs under that regulation means identifying significant health needs, prioritising them, and identifying resources potentially available to address them; required input includes at least one governmental public health department or State Office of Rural Health and members of, or organisations representing, medically underserved, low-income, and minority populations.

Rothman's typology of community organising comprises three broadly stated strategies: locality development, which pursues change through the active participation of diverse people and builds organisational capacity; social planning, a technical planning and problem-solving process assisted by professional experts; and social action, which organises disadvantaged people and communities to press the wider community for more resources or better treatment.

Rothman later revised his own typology: in a 2007 paper in the Journal of Community Practice he set out a multidimensional formulation comprising nine variants of practice, breaking out three distinct forms each of social planning/policy practice, capacity development, and advocacy, with some modes unidimensional and others combining strategic elements, and argued the modes need not be seen as conflicting.

Rothman's threefold taxonomy is also treated as superseded from outside his own work: Speer and Han state that the early taxonomy identifying social planning, locality development, and social action no longer holds, because organising efforts are now conceptualised through goals, methods, tactics, constituents, or issues under many labels including faith-based, labor, youth, neighborhood, identity-based, and democratic organising.

Community organising in the United States has roots in the settlement house movement and in Saul Alinsky's pragmatic organising; organising of this kind proceeds from the causal assumption that systems create social problems and that systems change requires the exercise of power, in contrast to approaches that treat the social system as fair and the problem as an individual information deficit; Alinsky's Rules for Radicals (1971) describes the organiser's dispositions rather than a fixed technique.

A recurring critique of contemporary organising is that professionalisation marginalises non-professional organisers and that dependence on government and large-foundation grant funding reduces a community organisation's control over its own mission.

Top-down community work brings expertise, funding, and legitimacy but risks reflecting the worldview of outside experts, losing community voice, and reinforcing existing power structures; bottom-up work originates with community members; neither is uniformly better and the two are often combined.

Asset-based community development identifies a community's existing strengths in order to mobilise local partnerships, and asset mapping is its first operational step, producing an inventory of tangible and intangible health-promoting features; McKnight and Kretzmann's critique of deficit framing is the conceptual foundation of that shift.

A documented pitfall of asset mapping and community consultation is relying on accessible 'easy voices' and strong gatekeepers, which compromises equity and produces an incomplete and biased picture; practitioners are advised to plan stakeholder identification by influence and interest and to use multiple entry points to reach often-missed groups.

Short-term, grant-funded community assets are transient and date an asset map quickly, and even where community dialogue occurs the link between community insight and actual resource allocation or policy response is often weak.

Asset-based community development has been criticised on structural grounds: MacLeod and Emejulu argue that in some hands it recasts structural inequality as a matter of individual or community responsibility and can be used to legitimise reductions in public provision.

Community-based participatory research is defined by AHRQ's evidence report as a collaborative approach that combines methods of inquiry with community capacity-building strategies to bridge the gap between knowledge produced through research and what is practised in communities.

In that review of 60 CBPR studies, steering committees and advisory boards were the main mechanisms for sharing research decision-making but generally did not develop the research questions or proposals; many studies had strong community-institution collaborations, relatively few combined that with solid research methods, and of 30 intervention studies only 12 had been completed and evaluated.

A review of the empirical coalition literature from 1980 to 2004 found 26 qualifying studies; of the 26 effectiveness indicators they used, 19 (73 percent) measured coalition functioning and only two (7 percent) measured change in community-wide health behaviour rates.

Six coalition-building factors were associated with effectiveness indicators in five or more of those studies: formalisation of rules and procedures, leadership style, member participation, membership diversity, agency collaboration, and group cohesion; the authors cautioned against strong conclusions given inconsistent measurement and reliance on cross-sectional designs.

A meta-analysis of 131 randomised and non-randomised controlled trials of community-engaged public health interventions for disadvantaged groups in OECD countries found positive pooled effects on health behaviour (d = 0.33), health consequences (d = 0.16), self-efficacy (d = 0.41), and perceived social support (d = 0.41), but found insufficient evidence to establish that any one model of community engagement outperforms another.

The Accountable Health Communities Model, which ran from May 2017 to April 2023 with 28 bridge organisations, funded bridge organisation infrastructure and staffing rather than the community services themselves; its evaluation found that navigation did not significantly increase the rate of connection to community service providers or the rate of need resolution relative to a randomised control group, and that where connections were made the available resources were often insufficient to resolve the need.

Speer and Han argue that an inflated focus on individual-level metrics for evaluating organising, alongside technocratic influence and faith in digital data, de-emphasises the social relationships through which organising builds collective power, so that common evaluation tools can miss what organising is actually doing.
Community organising is commonly taught as a repeating cycle of assessment, research, action, and reflection, and practitioners are advised that systemic change takes time to become visible.

Community coalitions bring together residents and public and private organisations to work on problems larger than a single partnership can address, typically agreeing a mission, vision, and shared values and writing action plans carried out by the coalition or by affiliated organisations; partnerships of any kind carry a risk of iatrogenic effects.

positions: O'Mara-Eves and colleagues report solid pooled evidence of positive effects on health behaviour and related outcomes across 131 controlled trials.

The Accountable Health Communities evaluation, a large randomised test of one specific community-connection mechanism, found no significant effect of navigation on connection rates or need resolution.
Zakocs and Edwards found that the coalition literature has almost never measured community-wide behaviour change at all.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports all three: engagement-based interventions as a broad class have positive average effects on individual-level outcomes, no particular model has been shown superior, and specific community-level mechanisms can and do fail. It does not claim that community practice as such is proven effective.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is asset-based community development empowering or a way of shifting responsibility?
positions: Practice-oriented public health literature treats asset mapping as a way to recognise communities as active partners with knowledge, networks, and resources rather than passive recipients.
MacLeod and Emejulu argue ABCD can capitulate to individualisation and privatisation and be used to justify cuts to public provision.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are stated. The lesson presents ABCD as a real methodological shift and the structural critique as a live, unresolved disagreement, without endorsing either political reading.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How should Rothman's typology be presented?
positions: It is widely taught and used in the field as three distinct models: locality development, social planning, social action.
Rothman himself replaced the threefold scheme in 2007 with a nine-mode formulation in which modes mix and are not treated as conflicting.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the three models because students will meet them, and states plainly that the author revised them toward mixed and overlapping modes.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about community practice at all; its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate about defining a term, checking context, and applying it to an example.
The draft's vocabulary list defined community practice circularly as 'a foundational Social Work & Human Services concept covered in this lesson', which is not a definition.
The draft's three quick-check items tested generic study skills rather than any community practice content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with researched content on community definition, Rothman's models and his revision, organising traditions, ABCD, community needs assessment, CBPR, coalitions, power analysis, and evaluation.
Added the attribution and the revision note for Rothman, which a typical secondary summary omits.
Added the structural critique of ABCD rather than presenting it as uncontested best practice.
Replaced any implied claim of effectiveness with the actual state of the evidence, including a large null finding.
Added an explicit educational-material statement and removed anything that could read as organisational or political advice.
rightsIssues: Alinsky's Rules for Radicals (1971) is in copyright. It is described and attributed; no text from it is reproduced, and it is not listed as a source record because it was not read directly for this lesson.

Kretzmann and McKnight's Building Communities from the Inside Out (1993) was not obtained directly. ABCD is attributed to them by name, and the substantive claims are sourced to the peer-reviewed asset-mapping literature that describes and cites their work.

Rothman 2007 and Zakocs and Edwards 2006 are paywalled. Only publisher metadata and the published abstracts were read, via Crossref, OpenAlex, and the Europe PMC REST API; both are REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording is reused.
MacLeod and Emejulu 2014 was read via the University of Edinburgh repository record; the published article is paywalled. REFERENCE_ONLY.

The AHRQ evidence report is in the public domain but is dated 2004 and is marked by NCBI Bookshelf as provided for historical reference; the lesson dates it and treats its findings as a snapshot of the CBPR literature to 2004, not as current.

Three source records (the CHNA regulation, the CMS Accountable Health Communities page, and Renaud et al. 2023) are reused unchanged from the project's verified source registry, with identical ids and URLs.
All prose is original. No source wording is adapted.

sourceRecords.title: What Is Community? An Evidence-Based Definition for Participatory Public Health
sourceRecords.provider: MacQueen KM, McLellan E, Metzger DS, et al.; American Journal of Public Health 91(12):1929-1938
sourceRecords.notes: Read via PubMed Central. Supports the multi-dimensional definition of community (locus, sharing, joint action, social ties, diversity), the derived common definition, the study base of 118 interviews across four populations between December 1995 and September 1998, and the finding that different groups weight the elements differently. Copyright American Journal of Public Health; nothing quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Trilogies: Lessons from 50 Years Facilitating Community-based Health Assessments and Planning in Appalachia
sourceRecords.provider: Behringer B; Journal of Appalachian Health 6(1-2):149-163, East Tennessee State University
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC REST API. Supports the working descriptions of Rothman's three strategies (locality development, social planning, social action) and their use as a strategy-selection device by community groups; the article cites Rothman's Planning and Organizing for Social Change (Columbia University Press, 1974) as the source of the trilogy. Also supports the observation that groups arrive with favoured strategies before comparing options. Facts synthesised; no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: Multi Modes of Intervention at the Macro Level
sourceRecords.provider: Rothman J; Journal of Community Practice 15(4):11-40
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher page returns 403 to automated fetchers. Supports only the fact and shape of Rothman's own revision: a multidimensional formulation of nine variants building on his earlier threefold concept, with three forms each of social planning/policy practice, capacity development, and advocacy, some unidimensional and some combining strategic elements, and his statement that the modes need not be seen as conflicting. Full text not obtained; no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: 26 CFR 1.501(r)-3 - Community health needs assessments
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Federal Register / Internal Revenue Service, via eCFR
sourceRecords.notes: Reused unchanged from the project source registry and re-verified for this lesson through the eCFR renderer API. Supports the five required CHNA steps, the three-year cadence and the implementation strategy adopted by an authorized body, the definition of assessing community health needs as identifying, prioritizing, and matching resources to significant needs, the required input sources, and - used here and not in the individual needs-assessment lesson - the rule that a hospital facility may take geography, target population, and principal function into account when defining its community but may not define that community so as to exclude medically underserved, low-income, or minority populations living in the areas from which it draws patients.

sourceRecords.title: How to do (or not to do)... asset mapping in community health
sourceRecords.provider: Chen X, Ye E, Fong N, et al.; Health Policy and Planning 41(3):513-526, Oxford University Press
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC REST API. Supports the definition of asset-based community development and asset mapping, the placement of assets in tangible and intangible categories, the attribution of the deficit critique to McKnight and Kretzmann, the boundary-definition problem, stakeholder identification by influence and interest, the 'easy voices' and gatekeeper pitfalls, the transience of short-term grant-funded assets, and the observation that links between community insight and actual resource allocation remain weak. Facts synthesised; no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: What explains community coalition effectiveness? A review of the literature

sourceRecords.notes: Published abstract read through the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 16530624); full text is paywalled. No wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: The effectiveness of community engagement in public health interventions for disadvantaged groups: a meta-analysis
sourceRecords.provider: O'Mara-Eves A, Brunton G, Oliver S, Kavanagh J, Jamal F, Thomas J; BMC Public Health 15:129
